facts.fact_text: Both applicants are political activists and opposition leaders.
The first applicant is a well-known anti-corruption campaigner.
The second applicant is a leader of the political movement "Solidarnost".
On 5 December 2011 the applicants took part in a public demonstration (a meeting) at Chistyye Prudy, Moscow.
The public demonstration on 5 December 2011 was held to protest against the allegedly rigged State Duma elections.
The demonstration on 5 December 2011 had been duly authorised by the mayor of Moscow.
The number of participants at the meeting on 5 December 2011 was estimated between 5,000 and 10,000.
The meeting on 5 December 2011 was conducted by the second applicant.
During the meeting on 5 December 2011, the first applicant addressed the participants with a speech calling for fresh, fair elections.
During the meeting on 5 December 2011, the first applicant described United Russia, the election frontrunner, as "a party of crooks and thieves".
After the demonstration on 5 December 2011, the applicants were arrested.
Both applicants were arrested at about 8.45 p.m. on 5 December 2011.
The applicants were charged with an administrative offence for refusing to comply with a lawful order of the police, in breach of Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
On 6 December 2011 the Justice of the Peace found the second applicant guilty of having disobeyed a lawful order of the police.
The second applicant was convicted under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences and sentenced to fifteen days' administrative detention.
On 6 December 2011 the Justice of the Peace found the first applicant guilty of having disobeyed the lawful order of the police.
The first applicant was convicted under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences and sentenced to fifteen days' administrative detention.
On 7 December 2011 the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow dismissed the applicants' appeals and upheld the first-instance judgment in both cases, citing the same reasons.

The Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004) provided, at the material time, that a public event could be stopped if there was a real threat to life or the physical integrity of persons or property.

The Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004) provided, at the material time, that a public event could be stopped if the participants had acted unlawfully or the event organiser had knowingly breached the requirements of the Act as regards the conduct of the event (section 16).

Under the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), a representative of the public authority, who had to be present at the event, could order the event organiser to put an end to the event in circumstances justifying stopping the event.

Under the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), the representative of the public authority had to explain the reasons for the order to end the event and provide time for compliance with it.

Under the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), if the organiser did not comply with the order to end the event, the public official could issue the same order to the participants.

Under the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), if both the organiser and participants failed to comply with the order to end the event, the police were to take appropriate measures to stop the event (section 17).

Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001, at the material time, provided that failure to obey a lawful order or demand of a police officer in connection with the performance of their official duties related to maintaining public order and security, or impeding the performance by them of their official duties, shall be punishable by a fine of between 500 and 1,000 Russian roubles or by administrative detention of up to fifteen days.

Article 27.2(1) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that the escorting or the transfer by force of an individual for the purpose of drawing up an administrative offence report, if this cannot be done at the place where the offence was discovered and if the drawing up of a report is mandatory, shall be carried out by the police.

Article 27.3(1) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that administrative detention or short-term restriction of an individual's liberty may be applied in exceptional cases if this is necessary for the prompt and proper examination of the alleged administrative offence or to secure the enforcement of any penalty imposed by a judgment concerning an administrative offence.
According to the Government, the group of about sixty people walked along the road, obstructing the traffic and chanting slogans such as "This is our city!" and "Down with the police state!".
According to the Government, at the crossroads of Pushechnaya and Rozhdestvenka Streets the police blocked the march and ordered the marchers to stop.
According to the Government, the marchers were stopped by the police again at 2 Teatralnyy Proyezd.
According to the Government, the marchers ignored the repeated demands of the police to stop and thereby prevented the police from carrying out their mission of securing public order.
According to the Government, confronted with the marchers' persistent behaviour, the police arrested the applicants.

Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001, at the material time, provided that failure to obey a lawful order or demand of a police officer in connection with the performance of their official duties related to maintaining public order and security, or impeding the performance by them of their official duties, shall be punishable by a fine of between 500 and 1,000 Russian roubles or by administrative detention of up to fifteen days.
Both applicants are political activists and opposition leaders.
The first applicant is a well-known anti-corruption campaigner.
The second applicant is a leader of the political movement "Solidarnost".
On 5 December 2011 the applicants took part in a public demonstration (a meeting) at Chistyye Prudy, Moscow.
The public demonstration on 5 December 2011 was held to protest against the allegedly rigged State Duma elections.
The demonstration on 5 December 2011 had been duly authorised by the mayor of Moscow.
The meeting on 5 December 2011 was conducted by the second applicant.
During the meeting on 5 December 2011, the first applicant addressed the participants with a speech calling for fresh, fair elections.
The applicants claimed that at the end of the meeting they had headed, with other people, towards the Kuznetskiy Most metro station, where the first applicant had left his car.
The applicants claimed that they were walking along the pavement, leaving the road clear for traffic.
The applicants claimed that their way was suddenly blocked by the riot police (сотрудники внутренних войск и ОМОН).
The applicants claimed that without any introduction or demand, the police surrounded a group of about one hundred protesters, including the applicants, pressing them against a building.
The applicants claimed that the surrounded group chanted "One for all, and all for one!".
The applicants claimed that the riot police then began to arrest the protesters.
According to the applicants, no one in the surrounded group put up any resistance.
The applicants claimed that they obeyed the police and followed them to the police bus.

The charges against the applicants were based on the identical statements of two police officers, identified as I. and F., who alleged that they had ordered the applicants to follow them to the police bus to give statements on the administrative offence.
Police officers I. and F. alleged in their statements that the applicants had pushed them away and had therefore been arrested.
The second applicant testified that he had been arrested at the indicated address while walking alongside other people returning from the authorised meeting.
The second applicant insisted that he had been arrested without any warning or orders from the police.
Witness B. testified that the policemen had not given the second applicant any orders before arresting him.
The Justice of the Peace based her findings against the second applicant on the witness statements of police officers I. and F., their written reports and the report on the administrative arrest.
The Justice of the Peace dismissed the testimonies given by the second applicant and witness B. on the grounds that they had contradicted the police officers' testimonies and reports.
The second applicant was convicted under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences and sentenced to fifteen days' administrative detention.
The Justice of the Peace dismissed all of the first applicant's requests except the request that witnesses T. and A. be called.

The Justice of the Peace disallowed the following questions put by the first applicant's defence counsel to police officers I. and F.: "What orders did you personally give to Mr Navalnyy?", "Who gave the order to arrest Mr Navalnyy?" and "Why were two policemen's reports identical?".
The first applicant testified that he had been returning from the authorised meeting, walking together with other people, not marching or chanting any slogans.
The first applicant testified that the police had repeatedly obstructed their way and had then arrested them.
The first applicant insisted that he had not received any orders from the police and had not resisted the arrest.
Witness T. testified that he had seen the first applicant's arrest.
Witness T. testified that it had been noisy and he had not heard the police officers giving the first applicant any orders before arresting him.
Witness T. testified that the police had announced through a loudspeaker "Your actions are unlawful" while surrounding a group of people, and had then begun arresting them.
Witness T. testified that he had not seen the first applicant resisting the arrest.

The requests to admit the video recordings were dismissed on the grounds that the court had no technical means of playing the recordings and that it would be unacceptable to use the devices provided by the defence.
The requests to admit the video recordings were not joined to the case file on the grounds that they had been submitted at the wrong stage of the proceedings.
On 6 December 2011 the Justice of the Peace found the first applicant guilty of having disobeyed the lawful order of the police.

The Justice of the Peace dismissed the testimonies of the first applicant, witness A. and witness T. on the grounds that they had contradicted the police officers' testimonies and reports, and that no reasons for mistrusting the latter had been established.
The first applicant was convicted under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences and sentenced to fifteen days' administrative detention.
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow dismissed the complaints about the refusals to hear witnesses and to admit the evidence requested by the applicants.
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow rejected the applicants' requests to have witnesses called in the appeal proceedings.
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow rejected the request to admit the video recordings in evidence because of their "unknown provenance".
On 7 December 2011 the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow dismissed the applicants' appeals and upheld the first-instance judgment in both cases, citing the same reasons.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow found that no bias on the part of police officers I. and F. or grounds for them to slander the first applicant had been established, and therefore rejected the explanations of the first applicant and the witness testimonies of A. and T. for want of reliable corroboration.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow found the second applicant's witness testimony unreliable and dismissed it because it contradicted the testimonies of police officers I. and F., which were described as logical, consistent, concordant and objectively corroborated by the written evidence.
